https://www.baltictimes.com/a_european_b.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive A European bank's operations in Russia are cynical and criminal - Paet 2026-07-22 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - According to Urmas Paet, Vice-Chair of the European Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, it is cynical and criminal for any European bank to be operating in Russia now, when Russia's war against Ukraine has been ongoing for years. "It is strange and painful to read the comments from the former head of the Estonian Financial Supervision Authority, Kilvar Kessler, suggesting there is nothing special about the continued operations in Russia of Hungary's OTP Bank, which is seeking to acquire Luminor, simply because other major European banks also operate there," Paet noted. "For a European bank to operate in Russia now, when the Russian war against Ukraine has been ongoing for years, claiming many lives, and while Russia's hybrid war against Estonia and all of Europe continues, is exceptionally cynical and criminal. Yes, there are still a few banks in Europe that are completely indifferent to Russia's slaughter of the Ukrainian people. But the majority of European banks left the Russian market long ago," he said. "Hungary's OTP Bank, which is acquiring Luminor, is one of those few European banks that continues its cynical business in Russia, just as the Hungarian government led by Orban has done for years. OTP Bank was also on the sanctions list imposed by Ukraine as a business entity supporting Russia's war against Ukraine. If this deal goes through and OTP does buy Luminor, then I can't imagine which Estonian customers would want to do any business with a bank that is indifferent to Russia's war against Ukraine," Paet remarked. The five people allegedly worked for Russian intelligence services to “conduct attacks and murders around the world, including in the United States,” the DOJ said in the indictment, adding the individuals were ‌still ​at large. The DOJ said Russian national ⁠Yuri Khrameev, 63; his son, ⁠Kirill Khrameev, 27; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, were charged with an alleged ​conspiracy to finance terrorism. Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. “Until ⁠we hear and see any ⁠credible evidence and arguments based on tangible ​facts, we do not believe it is necessary to ​comment on these reports,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told ‌reporters on Wednesday. Russia has previously denied conducting such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters the plots included “efforts to ⁠murder a Russian dissident who investigators believed was located in the Washington, D.C., area.” According to the Justice Department, the network ⁠allegedly recruited multiple ‌people in the United States to provide ⁠surveillance on Russian dissidents, including one living ​in ‌the U.S. and one in Lithuania. One recruit ​was allegedly ⁠offered “$40,000 to ‘eliminate’ or ‘disappear'” a person residing in the U.S., according to the Justice Department. Last year, another U.S. recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania, it said. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Manufacturing sector Drive reindustrialisation from No 10 North or risk failure, MPs tell Burnham Ninety-plus Labour MPs warn civil service lacks skills to drive growth where it is needed and plan should be steered by Louise Haigh from Manchester Business live – latest updates Heather Stewart Economics editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.42 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said. The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode” . John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”. France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation Read more However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work. “The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says. The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues. The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy . And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry. Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.” Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.” He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel , adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.” A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.” In its industrial strategy , published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence. In his conference speech, to which Healey had invited a young apprentice who had worked on building a new Mersey ferry, the chancellor said Labour would “get Britain growing. With hope for our young people.
